summary.text: A mapped overland flow path crosses this parcel; Auckland Council says these are routes where water naturally flows across the ground, and water can build up and enter homes if a path is blocked.

The council's shallow landslide susceptibility layer gives this area a High rating, and Auckland Council says these regional ratings are not a measure of landslide risk on individual properties and do not predict if or when a landslide might happen.
LINZ records the title as Leasehold, a title type for which this report has no background notes.
Based on what you told us, the building dates from a later year than the council's property category, which gives 1975; this report uses the council figure.
Based on what you told us, the cladding is monolithic, a plaster-style system that Settled.govt.nz discusses in its guidance on leaky buildings; no free public source could confirm the cladding.

next_steps.text: Ask whether the cladding is monolithic and consider a pre-purchase building inspection.
Ask the council or a drainage engineer whether the mapped overland flow path crosses this property and what the mapping means for it.
Ask insurers about past claims and flood exclusions before making an offer.
Ask your lawyer to obtain and review the LIM report and other property documents from the council.
Check the council property file for geotechnical reports, or ask a geotechnical engineer for site-specific advice.
Ask your lender what insurance evidence it requires and get insurance quotes early.
Check your private insurance policy for cover above the Natural Hazards Commission cap.
Ask your insurer and the Natural Hazards Commission which parts of the land are covered.
Ask your insurer about its own excess in addition to the Natural Hazards Commission excess.
Ask your insurer how the Natural Hazards Insurance levy appears in the quoted premium.
Ask a registered valuer about a current market valuation.
Ask your lender and lawyer what finance and insurance arrangements to confirm for an auction.
